Latest Update: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits.
  • But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S.
  • But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line.Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance.

But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy.

But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.”.

Budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already said the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034.

In a recent development, zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected demand. More than 1.1 million beneficiaries in the U.S. have signed up for discounted GLP-1s under a pilot introduced this year, allowing patients to access the drugs for reasons other than Type-2 diabetes.

It has been revealed that “On net, we estimate Medicare coverage of GLP-1s for weight loss will add close to $18 billion to the deficit by 2034. This is roughly 0.9% of the annual deficit, but a much smaller share of GDP, only about 5bps. The cumulative cost over 2026-2034 comes to around $107bn, about three times greater than the CBO’s estimate,” Zwemmer wrote.

From a macroeconomic perspective, there are also benefits to the government in supporting access to these medications. Zwemmer notes that up to 480,000 more Americans could be working by 2030 thanks to improved health. This would contribute a meaningful lift to payrolls and taxable incomes in a labor force shrinking due to aging and lower immigration.

Individual households that use GLP-1s could also see changes in their personal finances.

According to recent reports, A 2024 study by Cornell and Numerator found that households with at least one GLP-1 user reduced their grocery spending by 5.3% within six months of adoption. Most categories saw spending declines, but the largest reductions were concentrated in calorie-dense, processed categories, including a 10.1% decline in savory snacks.

Recent findings suggest that the change in consumer behavior is so marked that GLP-1s are helping “keep a lid on food inflation,” Oxford Economics added. Zwemmer writes: “We estimate that GLP-1-using households will reduce their annual spending on food both at home and away from home by a combined $500.”.

Zwemmer also notes that some of those funds may be diverted into buying new wardrobes, highlighting that new starters on GLP-1s are likely to spend $200 on refreshing their clothes. The U.S. economist added: “Scaled up to our estimate of nearly 40 million consumers entering 2027, this would translate to an $8bn uplift in apparel spending next year.”.

Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • Amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

The deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled looks to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy said on the organization’s earnings call last month.

Amazon declared the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Sources indicate that decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

Recent findings suggest that the deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

Amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

Industry observers note that the deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other massive buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

According to recent reports, “From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf mentioned in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano is facing fresh criticism for struggling to attract people and generate on-chain activity, despite being nearly nine years into its development.

Widely-followed crypto analyst Lark Davis has branded the network a “largely failed blockchain,” pointing to a stark adoption gap with Solana, which introduced four years later but has significantly outpaced ADA in daily owners, perpetual futures trading volume, and application revenue.

Despite having nearly a decade to establish itself in the blockchain industry, Cardano continues to face questions about its ability to attract users and generate meaningful network activity. Analyst Lark Davis has commented on the adoption gap between Cardano and Solana, arguing that Solana has significantly outperformed ADA despite launching four years later.

“Nine years in and Cardano is still waiting on adoption,” Davis wrote on X.

According to recent reports, according to Davis, Cardano accounts for just around 1% of Solana’s daily users, highlighting the stark difference in activity between the two networks. The gap reportedly extends beyond user numbers, with Cardano recording only about 0.3% of Solana’s perpetual futures trading volume.

In a recent development, the revenue figures paint an even more challenging picture for the Cardano ecosystem. Davis estimates that Cardano generates roughly 0.2% of the application revenue recorded across Solana’s ecosystem, further highlighting the difference in economic activity between the competing networks.

Based on these figures, Davis delivered a particularly harsh assessment of Cardano, describing it as a “largely failed blockchain.” His criticism centers on the contrast between Cardano’s nine-year journey and Solana’s ability to build a considerably larger user base and generate more trading activity and application revenue in a shorter period.

In a recent development, the latest criticism follows a series of similar remarks from Davis about Cardano’s adoption challenges. As ZyCrypto previously reported, the analyst had also taken aim at Cardano over its relatively small user base, questioning the network’s ability to attract and retain customers despite years of development.

Despite his harsh assessment of Cardano’s fundamentals, Davis has occasionally expressed optimism about ADA’s price prospects.

In November 2025, for instance, he suggested that Cardano could stage a rally similar to XRP’s 2024 surge, pointing to the strength of its community and brand as potential catalysts.

More recently, on September 28, Davis argued that Cardano’s “cult following” could help drive ADA back toward $1, with further upside potentially taking the token to $1.50 or even $2.

However, these bullish price projections focused more on speculative market demand and Cardano’s dedicated community than on measurable improvements in network adoption or ecosystem activity.

According to recent reports, XRP has lost 25.4% so far in November 2026, according to CryptoRank. Before this year, the token's biggest November loss was 23.3% in 2019, according to CryptoRank data, and the token lost another 16.8% in December 2019. On Nov. 22, XRP traded near $0.90, according to TradingView.

Sources indicate that the token also lost 10% and 11.8% in November of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In November of 2023 and 2024, XRP gained 1.4% and 281.7%.

According to recent reports, in November 2018, the crypto market crashed after the Bitcoin Cash hard fork, and XRP lost 19.3% that month. In December 2018, the token fell 2.25%. Two years earlier, XRP dropped 18% in November 2016 and 4.07% in December 2016.

XRP's median December return is -4.07%, and its average December return is +63.1%, according to CryptoRank data. Most of that average comes from December 2017, when XRP gained 818.9%.

XRP has closed December in the red in eight of the past 13 years. In December of 2021, 2022 and 2025, the token lost 17%, 16.9% and 14.8%, respectively, and in December 2024, it gained 6.94%.

In 2020, XRP's December drop came as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission sued Ripple on Dec. 22, 2020. The token lost 66.5% that month, and in January 2021, it gained 122.1%.

According to recent reports, in 2025, XRP's December drop came after the token set its all-time high of $3.65 on July 18, 2025. XRP lost 13.8% in November 2025 and 14.8% in December, and in January 2026, it fell another 10.6%.

It has been revealed that so far in 2026, XRP has lost value in seven of 11 months. The token's biggest monthly drops this year came in June and November, when it lost 22.1% and 25.4%, respectively, according to CryptoRank. Its best month was August, with a 30% gain.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 17, U.S. spot XRP ETFs had $1.08 billion in assets, according to SoSoValue. Since the start of November, the funds have lost about $26 million to outflows, and $19.13 million of that amount left in the week ending Nov. 13. Ripple's next monthly escrow release of 1 billion XRP is scheduled for Dec. 1.

According to recent reports, ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse also commented on the sell-off on CNBC on Nov. 19. "What happens is you've got risk-on assets and people are taking liquidity out of a very liquid market, crypto included — Bitcoin, XRP — and moving it into SpaceX. The exact same thing happened coming into the Anthropic IPO. What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets. I think you'll see that happen here as well," he said.

XRP's November drop took the token to its lowest level in two years, according to TradingView data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Launching in time for Spark Season, the Soneil group's holiday gift to EV drivers.

BRAMPTON, ON, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Soneil Spark, the EV charging business of Soneil Electronics, today publicly launched Spark Cashback, a program that turns the Clean Fuel credits your home charging creates into cash in your pocket. It releases alongside Spark Season, the Soneil group's way of giving back to EV drivers this holiday season.

"We've spent more than 30 years building power electronics people can rely on, and Spark Cashback puts that to work for everyday drivers," remarked Sonya Jain, CEO of Soneil Spark. "The charger is free with a deposit you get back, and every charge puts money back in your pocket. Spark Season is how we give back, with a gift that keeps giving and is even better shared with someone you care about.".

According to recent reports, under Canada's Clean Fuel Regulations, fuel suppliers must buy compliance credits, and charging an EV at home creates them. Your Spark charger tracks each session over Wi-Fi, Soneil Spark sells the credits, and you get a share as cash by Interac e-Transfer. The fuel industry helps offset your everyday charging, while you keep driving without tailpipe emissions.

Free, because your deposit comes back.

Industry observers note that the charger is free with a refundable deposit. Once you reach 1,250 kWh, the full deposit comes back, earlier than most comparable free-charger programs. You end up with a home charger that cost you nothing, apart from shipping, plus cash back on top. How soon depends on your driving.

Built on 30 years in power electronics.

A program is easier to trust when you know who is behind it. Soneil Spark designs and builds a complete range of EV charging under one roof, including mobile charging trailers for fleets and enterprise, all on our own technology, made in Canada, rather than rebadged off-the-shelf hardware. Soneil Electronics has reliably supplied batteries and chargers globally across a wide range of industries and applications, from golf carts and cleaning appliances to material handling and emergency power. The manufacturer has supplied more than 5 million chargers, and every Soneil Spark charger is backed by 24/7 North American-based support.

Spark Season: the gift that keeps giving back.

It has been revealed that pay it forward, in the most literal sense. Don't just tell the EV drivers you care about, get it for them. Family, close friends, anyone who drives electric can have a charger that's free with a refundable deposit and pays them back, with the fuel industry's compliance credits doing the giving.

Free charger requires a refundable deposit, plus shipping, refunded after 1,250 kWh of charging; timing depends on your driving. Promotional pricing and bonuses change throughout the season; readjustment on request, terms apply. The connection bonus is paid once, after the charger is connected and verified. Cash back is paid out at each payout milestone. Deposit and bonus amounts, rates, warranty terms and full terms are on the sign-up page. Comparisons are based on published terms of comparable free-charger deposit programs. Earnings are not guaranteed and are not income. Latest customers only.

Soneil Spark is the EV charging division of Soneil Electronics, a power electronics manufacturer with more than 30 years of experience, associated with Soneil Investments, a commercial property investment and asset management organization with more than $2.2 billion AUM. It designs and builds Level 2 home and commercial chargers, DC fast charging up to 480 kW, the Mobile EV Charging Trailer and Mobile Battery Energy Storage, made in Canada and available across North America. Learn more at soneilspark.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that deciding what to wear is one less thing on Matt Wood’s morning to-do list. Amazon’s AI chief has an AI agent for that.

Recent findings suggest that before he even wakes up, an AI agent has already checked his calendar and started figuring out what he should wear. The Amazon Web Services (AWS) chief AI and tech officer noted in a recent interview with Business Insider that his outfit-planning AI agent has become “somewhat famous internally.”.

Recent findings suggest that first, he connects AWS Quick to his calendar. The tool is typically used for business tasks like tracking regulations and finding supply chain problems. At around 4 a.m. each day, his AI agent scans his calendar, finds his most important meeting and suggests an outfit based on that information.

“I never want to be overdressed,” Wood told Business Insider. “I never want to be uncomfortable, and I definitely don’t want to make a decision on what I’m wearing before I’ve got my coffee.”.

He noted he usually drinks six cups of coffee before noon and is “useless” until he has had three.

It has been revealed that so how does this AI sartorial sidekick work, exactly? Wood connected the agent to a smart light bulb in his closet that flashes different colors. Each color represents a different type of day and a different outfit. For example, the light bulb might shine red for a keynote speaking engagement or blue for a day spent building things in the office.

He has arranged all of the clothes in his closet with matching color tags, so he simply picks an outfit with the same color as the light bulb. On a red-light day, for instance, that might mean a dark suit. On a blue-light day, that could mean something more casual, like jeans and a T-shirt.

According to recent reports, attire choices, however, are not the only way Wood uses AI to streamline his life. He noted that by his first cup of coffee, he is already reading an AI-generated briefing on the overnight news. His AI research agent pulls together updates from sources like X and Amazon communications. It gives him a simple report to review as he starts the day.

He also uses AI to prepare for meetings and develop new ideas. Wood remarked he has a “large crew” of agents that help him turn those ideas into things he can build.

Sources indicate that “Just this week, I’ve processed almost a billion tokens in AI usage, building things that I’m interested in or to help me with some of these other things,” Wood told Business Insider. (Tokens are units of data that AI models process, which allows them to reason through requests, per Nvidia.).

For context, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman mentioned earlier this month at a conference that the global average of token use is currently “about 100,000 tokens a month,” up from six years ago.

“If people can have a much higher quality of life, we want people to use a lot of AI,” Altman said. “This is just an unbelievable growth rate.”.

Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the newly introduced economy of shrinking labor shares

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t.
  • But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded, with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation.
  • In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t. Working Americans are taking home the smallest percentage of economic output, 52.8%, since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the metric in 1947.

But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded, with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation.

In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards.

According to recent reports, the consequences associated with shrinking labor shares are now becoming tangible. A recent Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that across the 11 states sampled, Amazon, the country’s largest tech giant by revenue, has 12,346 workers on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and 11,338 relying on Medicaid. That was nearly triple the number of Amazon employees in need of federal assistance compared to 2020, when GAO conducted a similar report. During that same period, Amazon saw an increase in annual profits from $11.6 billion to $77.7 billion. Amazon’s 2025 revenue soared 12% year over year, from $638 billion to a record $717 billion.

Amazon spokesperson Rachael Lighty told Fortune the conclusion drawn from the GAO report is “wrong,” and that it is misleading to look at raw numbers rather than percentages.

According to recent reports, “When you look at the actual facts, you see that Amazon pay is among the best in the industry, regular full-time employees have access to health care from their first day—at only $5 per week with $5 copays for employee-only coverage—and 74% of our regular full-time employees are enrolled in an Amazon health insurance proposal, well above the 65% private-sector take-up rate for full-time workers,” she stated in a statement. “We challenge other large retailers to provide the same Day 1 comprehensive health care benefits that we do.”.

Walmart and FedEx saw similar increases in the number of workers taking federal assistance, as did ride-share and delivery companies.

Kathryn Larin, director for education, workforce, and income security challenges at GAO, told Fortune the data illustrates that the Americans taking advantage of social safety net programs today are overwhelmingly in the workforce, with most working full-time. The income threshold for SNAP eligibility is about 130% of the poverty line, suggesting that despite many of these workers clocking in at their jobs, they still don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs.

It has been revealed that “What this analysis really points to is the large number of people who have very low incomes and continue to have very low income,” Larin said. “I mean, these are families that are really barely able to make ends meet, and yet they are working, and they are working a lot.”.

Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, recently warned of the hidden consequences of a shrinking labor share, particularly that despite economic indicators suggesting the economy is stable, most Americans are facing an ongoing affordability crisis. KPMG found in February that since 1982, corporate profits as a share of U.S. GDP increased from 8% to 15.85%. During that same period, employee compensation as a share of U.S. GDP shrank from 66.6% to 61.9%.

“This chart from my recent Economic Compass still haunts me,” Swonk mentioned in a social media post at the time. “A friend refers to it as the ‘revolution chart,’ which [is] disturbing but telling. Inequality fuels social and economic instability.”.

This trend has been about 50 years in the making, according to Anna Stansbury, an assistant professor of work and organization studies at the MIT Sloan School of Management.

Fewer workers in the U.S. are represented by unions—20.1% of U.S. workers in 1983 compared to 10.0% in 2025—giving them fewer opportunities to bargain for salaries and benefits, she noted. But more so, Stansbury blames the fissuring of the workplace, or the breakdown of the employer-employee relationship. In the past, the typical employer-employee relationship would be that of direct employment: A worker for a firm does their work at the company they are employed by. For example, a large bank like Bank of America used to employ a janitor to clean its offices.

But “in more and more cases, that’s not actually people’s experience of the workplace, particularly in lower middle-income jobs,” Stansbury told Fortune.

Instead, large workplaces like retailers and banks hire gig workers or subcontractors to complete jobs once done by direct employees: Companies hire a security provider, which employs a security guard to work outside that large company’s office. Delivery drivers are contract workers, not full-time employees.

As a result, companies don’t have to provide those workers equity or benefits. If a subcontractor violates labor law, the tech giant contracting them is not liable. In the meantime, these large companies are not only saving money on benefits, but are also getting to argue that they are increasing efficiency by not spending resources on workers whose roles are not directly driving revenue, Stansbury explained. A bank should employ bankers, not janitors, to get the most bang for its buck, the thinking goes.

It has been revealed that brent Neiman, a professor of economics at the University of Chicago, noted he believes AI has been the key driver of diminishing labor shares. In a New York Times op-ed, he argued the technology’s productivity promises pose the greatest threat to wages.

“Anyone who has used ChatGPT can see how much work now done by people could soon be done by technology,” he wrote.

Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok has already observed a correlation between AI adoption and lowered wages. In a white paper published in July, he and economist Sania Edlich found that among 321 occupations between 2015 and 2025, jobs with high exposure to AI saw a 6.7% decline in real wage growth after 2023 (following the wide release of ChatGPT), despite no employment changes, suggesting that while AI is not displacing jobs, it is associated with compressed wages. In other words, companies are seeing increases in productivity, but are using those increases as a cover to raise prices, while keeping wages stagnant.

Recent findings suggest that stansbury has a slightly different theory about AI. While the technology could begin to have an aggregate impact on the labor market, it’s still too early to say whether today’s shrinking labor share is part of a broader economic cycle, or if it’s a secular event, she remarked.

Sources indicate that unexpected inflation spikes, like what is currently happening, are usually associated with poorer real wages. If inflation is less volatile in the coming years and wage growth recovers, today’s trend of shrinking labor share could turn out to be cyclical, Stansbury said.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, Stansbury noted, a tightening labor market should increase labor share, and the labor market is already relatively tight. If inflation stabilizes, employment remains narrow, and the labor share increases, it will be a sign of an economic cycle completing itself. A bigger problem will be if wage growth stays low even if inflation improves and the labor market stays tight.

“If those two things happen and the labor share continues to fall,” she said, “then it would suggest that there’s actually been a secular shift, a secular acceleration in the downward trend.”.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Sept. 13, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that — Portal Space Systems, a Bothell, Wash.-based space manufacturer, has appointed Egbert Maben as principal satellite guidance, navigation and control (GNC) engineer — the startup’s first dedicated GNC hire. Maben joined from Blue Origin, where he was a leader in GNC and hardware integration and helped resolve mission-critical hardware failures. He also tackled assembly, integration and test, a process that verifies the performance of software and hardware components. He previously spent nearly two decades at Lockheed Martin.

In a recent development, maben, the manufacturer notes, has been keeping bees since ninth grade. “The only thing that’s left to see is whether Egbert, like bees, will be using dance to communicate those directives to our spacecraft,” Portal stated on LinkedIn.

— Seattle-based Yoodli has named Jessica Evans as its first mid-market sales leader.The startup recently expanded from helping people practice speeches, sales pitches and job interviews to providing corporate training across a wide range of skills. Evans joins from ClickUp.

— PATH, a Seattle-based global health nonprofit, has appointed three new board members:.

Sources indicate that — Ian McAllister joined Boston-based Toast as vice president of Product, Video AI, in October after the restaurant software organization acquired Airloom AI, the Seattle-area startup he founded and led as CEO. A longtime Seattle tech GM and product leader, he spent 12 years at Amazon and also held leadership roles at Airbnb and Uber.

McAllister remarked the idea for Airloom came when his wife, Sara McAllister, asked him to pick a security camera system for Allister, the Mercer Island restaurant and cocktail bar she owns and runs as GM. McAllister started Airloom AI to help restaurants use their existing video to improve the guest experience and operations. At Toast, he’ll continue that effort by combining Airloom’s technology with Toast’s platform. He’s building out Toast’s Vision AI team by hiring for multiple Seattle-based and remote product, engineering and AI/ML roles.

Blockstream CEO Adam Back has explained the overnight sell-off on Kraken's Canadian-dollar markets that sent the exchange's BTC/CAD pair to C$24,250, or roughly $17,000, on Saturday morning, and said that the drop started with the exchange's local USD/CAD market maker.

The Blockstream CEO addressed the issue on X on Saturday in a reply to a post that tracked large sell orders hitting Kraken's BTC/CAD order book at regular intervals throughout the night.

The $17,000 figure is based on the Bank of Canada's Friday rate of C$1.4325 per U.S. dollar. Kraken's BTC/CAD pair printed the C$24,250 low on Saturday morning, according to TradingView data.

"No, the reason was USDCAD Kraken local spot FX market-maker ran out of money, as it has depegged away from market rate 1.434," Back replied.

In the same post, the Blockstream CEO mentioned that it was "more accurate to say you could buy CAD discounted.".

Sources indicate that later, another X user argued that the Canadian dollar was in fact overvalued on Kraken during the sell-off, since anyone who held CAD could buy anything at a discount. Back agreed with the correction.

In a recent development, "You are right. BTCUSD normal price, USDCAD CAD mispriced, like a shortage of CAD bid the price up," Back wrote.

On Sunday, the Blockstream CEO described the whole chain of events in two more posts on X.

According to Back, if the USD/CAD market maker failed, there were few buyers of BTC in Canadian dollars, and so the BTC/CAD price fell. In his view, traders would normally close such a gap with an arbitrage trade "by selling USD to CAD to buy if it BTCCAD doesn't track BTCUSD.".

Back wrote that the drop "liquidated people" and triggered stop losses "based on a local false price.".

"And then USDCAD followed because you could buy BTC cheaply in CAD, so it became logical to buy CAD way over par to take that arb," he added.

The BTC/CAD pair recovered later on Saturday, and on Sunday, it traded at C$86,236 on Kraken, according to TradingView.

Kraken said in a statement that its Canadian-dollar trading pairs faced heavy selling pressure starting around 20:00 UTC on Friday, and prices on these pairs fell significantly below those on other markets.

Sources indicate that the Kraken sell-off started on the same day that Bitcoin dropped to $59,370, its lowest level since July 2, according to CoinGlass data. On Friday, CoinGlass also recorded $1.57 billion in liquidations across the crypto market over 24 hours, and long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of that amount.

Still, the exchange said that every order was processed correctly and that its security teams found no evidence of a breach or compromised accounts.

"Executed trades stand," Kraken said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Remember The Jetsons? Since the 1960s, humans have watched a world of flying cars, automated homes, and robotic assistants that seemed pure fantasy. Today, Elon Musk is working to bring elements of that future to life. And it isn’t just The Jetsons. The 2004 film I, Robot imagined humanoid robots and intelligent machines.

Twenty years later, when Tesla unveiled its Optimus robot, the film’s director, Alex Proyas, joked: “Can I have my designs back, please?”.

That raises a bigger question: If engineers are building the technology we saw in yesterday’s movies, who’s imagining the technology of tomorrow?

In a recent development, star Trek, for example, imagined communicators resembling mobile phones, voice-operated computers and medical scanning devices decades before they became everyday reality. These weren’t engineering blueprints; they were creative visions of what life might look like.

We celebrate the engineer, programmer and scientist who turn ideas into reality, but rarely the people who first imagined the possibility.

We have become obsessed with qualifications and specialization. We do need brilliant doctors, engineers and scientists, but mastering an existing discipline is not the same as imagining an entirely new one.

You can be an exceptional engineer or programmer and still struggle to imagine what the world will need in twenty years.

In a recent development, innovation requires more than knowing how to build something. It requires the instinct, faith and foresight to recognize what is worth building in the first place.

The greatest entrepreneurs are not necessarily those who understand every component of the technology they are developing. They are the people who can see beyond it, understand what people will want and bring together the talent capable of turning that vision into reality.

Artificial intelligence is transforming the economics of production and making powerful tools accessible to individuals who previously needed entire teams, specialist equipment and substantial financial resources. Quantum computing promises another leap in processing capability.

However, having access to powerful tools doesn’t automatically make someone an innovator. As the old saying goes, “A fool with a tool is still a fool.”.

When everyone has access to increasingly powerful technology, the real advantage belongs to those who know what to do with it, and, more importantly, can imagine what to do with it next.

According to recent reports, the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 identified creative thinking among the most important skills for the future workforce. The future isn’t a competition between technical and creative people; it’s about bringing those capabilities together, with imagination providing direction.

The next generation of world-changing entrepreneurs may come from filmmaking, storytelling, design, music or architecture, imagining experiences and industries we haven’t yet thought to ask for.

As we become fascinated by artificial intelligence and intelligent machines, we risk overlooking what makes us extraordinary: instinct, imagination, emotional intelligence, empathy and our ability to create stories that move people.

A machine can analyze millions of films, identify patterns and generate technically impressive productions, but the human experience that gives a story its meaning comes from living, loving, losing, believing, questioning and understanding the world through our own eyes.

For me, creativity is not simply a professional skill; it is one of the most fundamental expressions of being human.

There is a philosophical and spiritual dimension to this too. For those of us who believe in a Creator, if humanity was made in the image of an intelligent Creator, perhaps our own ability to create is one of the greatest gifts we have been given.

We weren’t simply created to consume what previous generations made. We were given the ability to imagine, design, build and create what comes next.

Our education systems need to reconsider what they are preparing the next generation for. We still teach people to enter existing industries and follow recognized career paths, when tomorrow’s greatest opportunities may not yet exist.

According to recent reports, who could have predicted the industries that would emerge from smartphones, social media, cloud computing and artificial intelligence? And who can confidently describe what will emerge from the technologies we are developing today?

Sources indicate that we need to encourage people to experiment, question, design and invent. Creativity should sit at the heart of entrepreneurship, science, medicine, architecture, business and technology.

Sources indicate that the next great medical breakthrough might be imagined by a filmmaker. The next revolutionary transport system might originate with an architect. The next billion-dollar technology company might begin with somebody who has never studied computer science.

Sources indicate that engineers will help make these visions possible. Entrepreneurs will recognize their potential and bring the right people together. But somebody has to imagine them first.

Today’s conversation about technology is too often dominated by fear: disappearing jobs, collapsing industries and what AI might take away from humanity.

These are legitimate questions, and we must take responsibility for developing technology safely, but fear cannot drive progress.

According to recent reports, we should really ask what we can create that was previously impossible. What industries can we build, what problems can we solve and what technologies can we imagine that make today’s inventions look primitive?

Working at the intersection of technology, media, storytelling and entrepreneurship has taught me that the greatest opportunities belong to those who connect imagination with possibility.

The next Elon Musk might not be sitting in an engineering laboratory. They might be writing a screenplay, designing a world, directing a film or simply imagining something that everyone else thinks is impossible.

The engineers may build the future, but it’s the visionaries who will imagine it first.

Twenty years later, when Tesla unveiled its Optimus robot, the film’s director, Alex Proyas, joked: “Can I have my designs back, please?”.

That raises a bigger question: If engineers are building the technology we saw in yesterday’s movies, who’s imagining the technology of tomorrow?

In the final stretch of 2026, some XRP Ledger protocol features await mainnet activation, with validator support and amendment voting as the final steps to bring new functionality to the XRPL network.

In light of this, three amendments are racing against the 2026 calendar, with only a few votes left to reach a majority and enter the two-week activation period. These include SingleAssetVault, LendingProtocol and confidential transfers.

All three remain below the required validator approval threshold of over 80% support, making the final weeks of the year increasingly important for their activation prospects.

With about five weeks left in 2026, activation remains possible this year, but additional validator support for each amendment must arrive soon enough and be sustained to complete the required two-week activation window.

Industry observers note that the lending protocol allows on-chain fixed-term, uncollateralized loans from pooled funds in a Single Asset Vault. There are two amendments: LendingProtocolV1_1 and the original Lending Protocol amendment.

It has been revealed that the focus is on LendingProtocolV1_1, which extends the Lending Protocol and SingleAssetVault amendments with a upcoming closed-ended vault and cash-basis accounting. With the amendment, new loan brokers can only be created against closed-ended vaults.

LendingProtocolV1_1 has reached 70.59% support with 24 out of 34 validators voting yes, according to XRPScan data. It needs 28 votes to reach a majority, or more than 80% of 34 votes, meaning it has just four votes left.

Recent findings suggest that A major privacy amendment for the XRP Ledger, confidential transfers, has 64.71% support and 22 of 34 validators voting yes. Confidential transfers, which rely on advanced cryptography (EC-ElGamal and ZKPs), offer institutional-grade privacy for Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs) and need six more yes votes to enter the activation window.

SingleAssetVault creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. It has gained 73.53% support so far with 25 out of 34 validators voting in favor. Reaching more than 80% of 34 votes requires 28 votes; thus, three votes remain for it to enter the activation window.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that “Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest, tells Fortune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows, a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that “Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest, tells Fortune. “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”.

According to recent reports, anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models, up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” states Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.”.

In a recent development, rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame, most high-performing models were either small academic releases or commercial systems with restricted outside access. The first open-weight models originated in academic research, where sharing model weights to ensure reproducibility was standard practice.

Sources indicate that in 2019, OpenAI went against tradition by initially withholding the full 1.5-billion-parameter version of GPT-2, citing risks of misuse such as disinformation, impersonation and phishing. Most U.S. frontier labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, keep the underlying parameters private, giving people access through apps or APIs rather than letting them download and run the models themselves.

Industry observers note that in the early years of generative AI, most users preferred closed-weight models because they delivered performance that open-weight alternatives could not match. Yet in recent years, the improved capability and cost-efficiency of powerful Chinese models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has swung the pendulum back in favor of open-weight models.

Industry observers note that “For the longest time, the idea has been that you can get the highest level of performance using closed-weight models, so many firms start off by using them,” says Hariharasudhan Saminathan, cofounder of Friday, a sovereign AI startup backed by global venture capital firm Antler. But now, “through distillation and other processes, open-weight models’ performance almost matches that of closed-weight models,” he says.

Industry observers note that “Many of our pipeline customers are now adopting open-weight models right off the bat,” he adds. “They’re not even touching the closed-weight ones.”.

It has been revealed that pinterest, for example, uses Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models to power its online platform. “We’ve driven down our inference costs using post-trained open-weight models,” Kim explains. “They offer over 90% cost reduction.” (Many leading Chinese open-weight models activate only a subset of parameters per token, cutting compute and energy needed per request.).

Sources indicate that kim also cites the flexibility of these models as a draw. Last October, the firm released Pinterest Assistant: an AI-powered tool that pairs a customized Qwen multimodal LLM with the firm’s proprietary Taste Graph, to generate shopping recommendations for customers based on their individual aesthetic preferences.

“[With open-weight technology], we can create a specialized model that actually does what we need it to do very effectively, which is understanding visual information,” claims Kim.

Rather than choosing one or the other, some firms are using a mix of open-weight and closed-weight AI models.

Industry observers note that eu Leong Oh, medical director at The Longevity Suite Asia, a Singapore-based wellness clinic, says he’s using Claude and Google’s Gemini to build the team’s in-house healthcare portal, but plans to pivot to open-weight models for daily use. “For things like prototyping, exploration and research, it’s still very useful to have a large-parameter, trained, closed-weight model,” Oh says.

Recent findings suggest that he compares a top-tier frontier model to a Michelin-starred chef. “You’ll want a chef like Gordon Ramsay to decide the processes in your restaurant, but you don’t need him to do the cooking all the time,” he indicates. “Similarly, within companies, a lot of the heavy lifting and token budget will eventually be taken over by more cost effective open-weight models.”.

Sources indicate that token costs are also skyrocketing with the rise of agentic AI. An AI agent might consume five times more tokens than a chatbot interface, because it runs multi-step loops rather than a single task. Those increasing costs may push companies to adopt cheaper open-weight models on top of existing closed-weight ones.

Recent findings suggest that “Companies are becoming more cost-conscious about their AI deployment,” indicates Srividya Jandhyala, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. “Not every task needs the power of a frontier model, and companies are recognizing that ‘good enough’ models work for a large variety of operations.”.

It has been revealed that yet a company’s decision whether or not to use an open-weight model could come down to politics, rather than cost or technical ability. The leading open-weight models come from Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba, and z.AI; their growing usage in both U.S. and global business is worrying some in Washington about China’s growing influence over the technology.

According to recent reports, “The American AI stack remains far stronger than China’s and we must continue to lead,” Representative John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the U.S. House’s Select Committee on China, wrote in a Sept. 23 statement.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 18, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was considering requiring U.S. firms to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, in hopes of discouraging use of the technology without imposing new restrictions that might anger Beijing.

In a Nov. 20 report, Moolenaar warned that American businesses were adopting inexpensive Chinese AI models. “Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap,” he wrote.

Cursor—whose Composer coding agent was built on Moonshot’s Kimi model—told Congress that it’s considering phasing out Chinese AI models due to “geopolitical risk,” CNBC reported.

“For global companies, especially in Western markets, there is a trade-off between cheaper Chinese alternatives versus concerns about continued access,” explains Jandhyala of ESSEC. “If they think that future policies may force them to reduce their reliance on Chinese AI models, companies may pre-emptively start using U.S. open- or closed-weight models.”.

According to recent reports, A handful of U.S. companies—including Thinking Machines, Reflection AI and Nvidia—are releasing open-weight models. Nvidia and its recently returned CEO, Jensen Huang, have also championed the technology. According to Reuters, Huang’s support for open-weight AI helped persuade Trump and Vice President JD Vance to push for his return.

The concern that Chinese models may come with hidden backdoors may be overstated, says Erik Cambria, a professor of AI at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University (NTU).

According to recent reports, “Concerns about Chinese models should be distinguished between genuine technical security risks and geopolitical perceptions,” he indicates. “An open-weight model deployed locally, without transmitting sensitive data externally, presents a very different risk profile from a remotely hosted API, regardless of the model’s country of origin.”.

Still, geopolitical concerns may drive companies to diversify where they get their models from. “Europeans optimize for sovereignty and compliance,” states Groth of UC Berkeley. “In Asia and the Gulf, pragmatists hedge across both stacks and refuse to pick a side, unless they need models and applications which implicate national security.”.

Sources indicate that for businesses, the goal may not be picking a winner in the AI race, but keeping their options open. “Businesses will combine models from different providers and select the most appropriate one for each workload,” says Cambria.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a 2026 Gartner survey, 87% of customers said companies using generative AI for customer service must provide access to a human agent.

That doesn’t mean customers are against AI. It means businesses need to think carefully about where they use it and where human support still matters.

In a recent development, every business was built on a dream, and that’s a deeply human thing. When we replace real care with automation in the moments that matter most, we risk chipping away at the very thing that made the business worth building.

So how do you know where AI belongs and which moments need protecting? Start by asking four questions, then test your answers.

Before using AI in any area of your business, ask these four questions:.

Industry observers note that if a behind-the-scenes task is predictable, simple and low-stakes, let AI handle it. If it’s personal, complex or high-stakes, keep a person in the loop.

It has been revealed that I recently heard from an AnswerConnect client, Craig Grove, founder of GRT Realty, who learned the hard way where not to put AI. He partnered with an AI answering service, only to realize his leads were hanging up on the robot. After switching to human phone answering, he grew his business from six real estate agents to 70.

Running the four questions tells you where AI could go. Testing tells you whether it’s actually working.

I’ve learned firsthand that even the best ideas benefit from a little testing before they’re rolled out more widely. I’m naturally someone who likes to take action, particularly when I’m confident something has potential. After a few instances where the direction or idea I had in mind wasn’t as great as I thought, I found myself in a place where I’d made mistakes.

In hindsight, I should have started smaller, talked to more people and got feedback first. I’ve never regretted taking a little extra time to test an idea before jumping in. AI deserves the same approach.

Look at it from two angles: your customers and your team.

Then make testing a habit. Things are constantly changing, including your customers’ expectations. What worked in January can fail by June.

AI is one of the most useful tools business owners have ever had. Used in the right place, it gives your people more time for the work that matters. Used in the wrong place, it erodes the trust your business was built on.

So ask the four questions, test the answers, and keep checking.

Your business was built on a dream. Use AI to help it grow, and keep people where your customers need them most.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering.
  • But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.

Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

It has been revealed that “We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya remarked. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”.

CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Industry observers note that twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

Sources indicate that “We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu said. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”.

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

“The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya remarked. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”.

According to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry noted have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry said.

Industry observers note that other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

Sources indicate that “Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”.

It has been revealed that his team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

Sources indicate that other inventions sought to get customers off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

It has been revealed that “I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae remarked. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”.

Recent findings suggest that also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

“The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev mentioned. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”.

His prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he plans to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

Sources indicate that “We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards said. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”.

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:.

This cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

To do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

Recent findings suggest that “We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat remarked. “Maybe even globally.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As 81.5 million Americans travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, conversations around the dinner table could present a rare opportunity for people to learn more about their aging loved ones. A upcoming class of AI startups wants to help them preserve those conversations forever.

Charlie Greene, the cofounder and CEO of Remento, first learned about the importance of recording memories when his father, Don Greene, died during the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 on 9/11.

A 10-year-old boy at the time of the terrorist attack, which resulted in his father’s plane crashing in Shanksville, Penn., the now 34-year-old Greene mostly has a collection of old home videos to remember him by.

In a recent development, so when his mother Claudette, 74, was diagnosed with stage-three lung cancer, he promptly acted to record her memories. With the intention of conducting an oral history interview, Greene searched “questions to ask a parent,” which Google morbidly autocompleted with “before they die.”.

When he started asking her the questions like “How did you get to elementary school as a kid,” she lit up, surprised he was interested at all.

“The thing that blew me away about that experience was how unmorbid it felt,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that claudette is in remission, but her battle with cancer still left Greene “unhealthily fixated” on the idea of how to best preserve loved ones’ memories. In October 2023, he launched Remento, which sends older “storytellers” a weekly text or email reminder prompting them to respond to photos or questions chosen in advance by their family members, such as, “What was the hardest thing you had to overcome as a child?”.

After gathering a maximum of a year’s worth of responses, the AI converts the raw transcript into a naturally flowing narrative that goes into a physical book complete with images and QR codes linking the text to the original recordings.

Greene told Fortune Thanksgiving presents a great opportunity for people to discover new memories or learn new twists on well worn stories from their relatives.

“One of the things I want for my daughter is the chance to sit next to her grandmother and hear her say ‘Believe it or not that’s me.’ Thanksgiving is a pretty good excuse to pull an old album off the shelf and make room for the two of them on the couch,” he mentioned.

Last year, Greene secured a $300,000 investment from billionaire Mark Cuban during an episode of Shark Tank in exchange for a 10% stake in his tech giant. He has raised a total of $4.3 million since launch.

Greene said he understands some people’s skepticism of AI, because “A lot of what AI is proposing to the world doesn’t feel actually that good to our lives right now.”.

It has been revealed that widespread anxiety about AI replacing human workers as well as concerns over its environmental footprint have contributed to some people’s increasing skepticism toward the technology. A March study of more than 3,000 people by the nonprofit Jobs For the Future found that 38% of respondents noted AI was doing more harm than good, while less than half said the technology was a net positive.

Yet Greene hasn’t gotten as much pushback about the manufacturer’s use of AI as he had expected because Remento is using the technology to provide its customers with something deeply personal, he added.

Sources indicate that “Investors want to invest in AI, because it’s an exciting place to be. But I think what we’re experiencing is people have problems and they want them solved, and they want consumer technology to be able to solve those problems,” he said.

Kindred Tales, a rival platform cofounded by Nick Hern and his wife Rebecca Hern, has seen a similar trend with their customers. The company has both AI and non-AI versions of its product.

While the non-AI version requires customers to type out their responses to weekly prompts, the AI version helps by providing speech-to-text transcription and some light editing. It can also write a first draft of the interviewee’s story, if they want.

Before 2025, just over half of the organization’s customers chose the AI version, but that number jumped to 80% after 2025.

“Customers increasingly see AI as a meaningful part of the storytelling experience, not just an extra,” Nick Hern told Fortune.

Part of the reason is that the company’s AI chatbot, called “Ali,” gives the interview process a conversational feel by teasing more out of owners with follow-up questions crafted to their responses.

Sources indicate that AI has helped Kern, who also works full time for Thomson Reuters, run the tech giant as well. He noted he has used the technology to help filter emails, as well as slowly replace freelancers that he previously hired to help him craft marketing and social content.

At a time when companies are spending billions to bring AI to every American, Greene, noted, despite its flaws, AI has allowed Remento’s customers’, as well as himself, to record moments with family members that are invaluable.

“AI in our tech giant is being used to get people to do things that they’ve always wanted to do but haven’t been able to, and to make that experience as seamless and humanlike as possible,” he said.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on April 25, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances.
  • The companies announced today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP).
  • The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances. sonnen and SOLRITE Energy are putting that same principle to work for the grid, adding smart breakers that can temporarily switch off selected household loads while batteries help meet electricity demand.

The companies announced today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP). The setup combines sonnenHub with breakers that manage power-hungry equipment, both during outages and when the grid needs help.

The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.

Industry observers note that A VPP connects home batteries into a network so they can work together as a larger energy resource. This addition gives SOLRITE another way to respond: in addition to controlling the batteries, it can reduce the amount of electricity that participating homes use.

It has been revealed that sonnen and SOLRITE used the example of a pool pump, as it’s energy-intensive, nonessential, and runs for longer periods. When an event begins, ADAPT temporarily switches off the pool pump while the sonnen battery sends electricity to the grid.

Sources indicate that with less battery power going toward the pump, more can flow to the grid. Across participating homes, that gives the VPP more flexibility than relying on battery dispatch alone.

Industry observers note that homeowners have to opt in to that grid participation, and ADAPT will switch off only pre-approved household loads. Joining the VPP program doesn’t give the operator blanket permission to turn off anything in the house.

“Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home,” mentioned Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy.

The breakers also tackle a practical problem with home backup: Significant appliances can drain a battery rapidly, and the surge of power some equipment needs to start can overload a backup system just as an outage begins.

ADAPT coordinates the smart breakers with the sonnen battery to automatically switch off large loads during backup operation. When grid power returns, it restores them, so homeowners don’t have to go around resetting individual circuits.

That also gives homeowners more flexibility later. According to the companies, changing which smart-breaker-controlled loads are switched off during an outage doesn’t require rewiring those circuits.

The installation benefit matters, too. Some backup setups require electricians to move selected circuits into a separate panel. This system manages compatible circuits where their breakers already sit, which the companies say reduces installation complexity and inspection work.

Whole-home backup still has limits. Automatically managing large loads helps the available battery capacity go further; it doesn’t mean every appliance can run at once throughout an outage.

Recent findings suggest that SOLRITE finances, builds, and owns residential solar-plus-storage projects through what it calls Virtual Power Plant Agreements, with no upfront cost to homeowners. It says it operates in Texas, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Illinois, with more markets planned.

Ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, Ripple USD (RLUSD), has now entered the top five stablecoins by market cap, reaching a latest all-time high in its circulating supply, a major milestone for the stablecoin less than two years after its launch. RLUSD went live in December 2024.

Sources indicate that RLUSD has surpassed World Liberty Financial USD (USD1), Global Dollar (USDG) and PayPal USD (PYUSD) to become the fifth-largest stablecoin in the world, according to data from CoinMarketCap. Only Tether’s USDT, Circle’s USDC, Ethena’s USDe, and Dai (DAI) are ahead of it.

The milestone is proof of the rapid growth RLUSD has experienced in a competitive stablecoin market dominated by established players like Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC.

RLUSD’s total circulating supply across the XRP Ledger and Ethereum has reached a new high, with $2.85 billion in circulation, according to Ripple’s stablecoin tracker.

In a recent development, ethereum commands $2.089 billion of this total figure, while $768 million in supply sits on the XRP Ledger. While Ethereum right now holds the larger share of RLUSD’s supply, XRPL has seen significant activity in RLUSD settlement volumes.

In March 2025, during a Bloomberg TV interview, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse projected that RLUSD would enter the top five stablecoins; that projection has now been fulfilled.

According to RWA Foundation, Ripple led weekly stablecoin growth, adding $75.4 million in the last seven days. This growth was reflected in RLUSD's market cap, allowing it to surpass World Liberty Financial USD to clinch the fifth spot in global stablecoin rankings.

Former Ripple executive Anthony Welfare highlighted this growth in a recent X post, saying, “RLUSD is the only major stablecoin growing right now.”.

Welfare noted that RLUSD supply is up nearly 20% in three weeks, rising from $2.42 billion to $2.9 billion, while USDT has fallen by $5 billion and USDC by $3 billion over the same period.

The XRP Ledger accounts for the majority of RLUSD settlements: in an analogy on X, Welfare noted that XRPL holds about 27% of RLUSD’s supply but processed 57% of its volume last week, amounting to $6.7 billion versus Ethereum, which recorded $5 billion.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making significant decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. That’s why I’m so passionate about supporting small businesses.”.

Industry observers note that the actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative rolled out this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

At the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A new docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

Sources indicate that and then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

Industry observers note that the stakes are big. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

An analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common concerns, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching fresh customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

“The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she stated. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”.

Sources indicate that 2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she stated.

In a recent development, 3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

Industry observers note that “Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she stated.

Recent findings suggest that 4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

Recent findings suggest that “You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she said. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”.

In a recent development, to see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the substantial-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.
